2026 is not waiting for the year-end retrospective. With the year barely half over, our database has already captured 42 woke-leaning films and shows from the calendar year -- six STRONGLY WOKE entries, fourteen WOKE, and five WOKE LEAN cracking the top 25. The range runs from The Moment's staggering 27.0 margin to Forbidden Fruits' relatively modest 6.6. The median hovers around 12.6 -- a solid WOKE verdict on a film that is just average for its year. This is the new baseline.

What distinguishes 2026 from 2025 is the nature of the ideological content. Last year's most woke entries were often animated features and horror films that smuggled politics inside genre packaging. This year's top entries are more direct. The Moment is a Charli XCX mockumentary produced by A24 that dispenses with narrative entirely in favor of progressive cultural celebration. Disclosure Day is Steven Spielberg -- the most commercially reliable director in American history -- making an alien-contact film that functions as an anti-institutional transparency parable. The Bride! reimagines a Universal monster as a feminist gothic romance. These are not hidden messages. They are the marquee.

The auteurs are heavily represented. Steven Spielberg, Boots Riley, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Olivia Wilde, Greta Gerwig, Kristoffer Borgli, Gregg Araki, David Lowery -- directors with established ideological signatures -- all released 2026 films on this list. A24 alone distributed six of the top 25 entries. Neon contributed two more. The prestige pipeline is now fully aligned with progressive messaging, and the alignment is production-level, not accidental.

The box office story for 2026 is still being written, but early indicators are worth noting. Several high-profile woke entries have underperformed expectations. Audiences are increasingly pattern-aware. The question for the second half of 2026 is whether the industry processes what the data is telling it or simply doubles down through awards season. Ranked from most woke to least woke.

STRONGLY WOKE (Margin 19.8 and Above)

#1: The Moment (2026)

Woke Score: 32.0 • Traditional Score: 5.0 • Verdict: STRONGLY WOKE • Margin: 27.0

Genre: Comedy | Platform: Theatrical | Distributor: A24

Let's be precise about what this film is: a $4 million mockumentary in which Charli XCX -- pop music's reigning progressive icon -- produces, co-wrote, and stars in a fictional version of her own real life, distributed by A24, the most ideologically consistent prestige label in American cinema. The "Brat Summer" phenomenon of 2024 -- lime green aesthetic, feminist anti-establishment messaging, explicit sexual identity celebration -- is not the backdrop of this film. It is the thesis. The Moment is essentially a feature-length victory lap for progressive pop culture, with a traditional score of just 5.0 reflecting how thoroughly it abandons any pretense of ideological balance. At a margin of 27.0, it is the most ideologically aggressive film of 2026 so far.

#2: Disclosure Day (2026)

Woke Score: 43.1 • Traditional Score: 18.3 • Verdict: STRONGLY WOKE • Margin: 24.8

Genre: Science Fiction, Thriller | Platform: Theatrical | Director: Steven Spielberg | Distributor: Universal Pictures | Rating: PG-13

Cast: Emily Blunt, Josh O'Connor, Colin Firth, Eve Hewson, Colman Domingo

Disclosure Day is Steven Spielberg's return to science fiction spectacle, but thirty years into his career, he is a different filmmaker than the man who made Close Encounters of the Third Kind. The wonder remains. The sense of awe before the unknown remains. But Spielberg's contemporary instinct is to frame the alien encounter through an institutional transparency narrative: the government has been lying, the truth must come out, and the people deserve to know. Emily Blunt anchors the film with genuine gravity, playing a scientist caught between state secrecy and public obligation. Josh O'Connor brings nervy intelligence as a journalist pushing for disclosure. At 43.1 woke and 18.3 traditional, the gap is enormous -- the wokeness is embedded in the film's core argument about institutional trust rather than surface-level messaging. The craft is undeniable, as you would expect from Spielberg. The politics are equally undeniable.

#3: The Bride! (2026)

Woke Score: 34.8 • Traditional Score: 10.4 • Verdict: STRONGLY WOKE • Margin: 24.4

Genre: Gothic Romance / Horror | Platform: Theatrical (IMAX)

Maggie Gyllenhaal's The Bride! is a film that tells you exactly what it is from the very first frame, and it does not care if you approve. Set in 1936 Chicago, the film reimagines the Bride of Frankenstein story as a feminist gothic romance about a murdered woman named Ida (Jessie Buckley) brought back to life by a female scientist, Dr. Cornelia Euphronious (Annette Bening). The Universal monster is repurposed as a vehicle for exploring female autonomy, bodily agency, and the violence inherent in the male gaze. Christian Bale's monster is both threat and sympathetic figure. Peter Sarsgaard and Penelope Cruz round out a cast that commits fully to Gyllenhaal's vision. The 34.8 woke score reflects an ideological project that touches every element of production design, character arc, and thematic resolution. At 24.4 margin, this is ideological filmmaking executed at a high level of craft.

#4: Hamlet (2026)

Woke Score: 30.2 • Traditional Score: 9.0 • Verdict: STRONGLY WOKE • Margin: 21.3

Genre: Drama / Tragedy | Platform: Theatrical | Director: Aneil Karia | Rating: R

Cast: Riz Ahmed, Art Malik, Sheeba Chaddha, Morfydd Clark, Joe Alwyn

Riz Ahmed's Hamlet is not your grandfather's Danish prince -- and that is precisely the point. Director Aneil Karia transplants Shakespeare's tragedy into a South Asian diasporic context, with Ahmed playing the melancholy prince as a man caught between ancestral obligation and personal identity. The casting is deliberately color-conscious, with the court of Elsinore reimagined as a multicultural power structure where race and lineage carry unspoken weight. The production is visually striking and Ahmed's performance is committed and intelligent. At 30.2 woke to 9.0 traditional, the film's progressive reframing is comprehensive -- this is not Shakespeare with diverse casting layered on top but Shakespeare reinterpreted through an identitarian lens from the ground up. Conservative viewers who love the play should know that this version is making arguments the original text does not make.

#5: The Pitt: Season 2 (2026)

Woke Score: 29.9 • Traditional Score: 9.9 • Verdict: STRONGLY WOKE • Margin: 20.0

Genre: Medical Drama | Platform: HBO Max

The Pitt Season 2 premiered January 8, 2026 on HBO Max, following the same format as Season 1: each episode covers roughly one hour of a single fifteen-hour shift at the Pittsburgh Trauma Medical Center. This season is set on the Fourth of July, which the writers use for the kind of dramatic irony that tells you exactly where the show's politics land. Noah Wyle is exceptional as Dr. Robby, giving one of the most committed performances on television. But the show's ideological architecture is unmistakable: the health care system is broken by design, the patients who suffer most are marginalized, and every institutional failure maps to a political choice. At 29.9 woke to 9.9 traditional, the margin of 20.0 reflects a medical drama that has fully committed to diagnosing America rather than just its patients. The craft is superb. The politics are the prescription.

#6: Leviticus (2026)

Woke Score: 23.8 • Traditional Score: 4.0 • Verdict: STRONGLY WOKE • Margin: 19.8

Genre: Horror / Romance / Coming-of-Age | Platform: Theatrical / Streaming | Director: Adrian Chiarella | Distributor: Neon (US) / Maslow Entertainment (International) | Rating: R (Sexual Content, Violence, Disturbing Images)

Cast: Joe Bird, Stacy Clausen, Mia Wasikowska, Jeremy Blewitt, Ewen Leslie

Leviticus is a competent horror film with a very clear ideological mission: to argue that religious communities opposed to homosexuality are not just wrong, but monstrous. The setup follows Naim, a new kid moving to a small religious town in rural Victoria after his parents' divorce. He befriends the pastor's son and the two develop a romantic connection that the community violently rejects. The horror elements -- and there are genuine horror elements -- are deployed in service of an allegory about religious sexual ethics as a literal monster. At 23.8 woke and just 4.0 traditional, the margin of 19.8 reflects a film whose ideological architecture leaves virtually no room for countervailing interpretation. The craft is competent. The argument is not subtle.

WOKE (Margin 9.8 to 19.0)

#7: I Love Boosters (2026)

Woke Score: 20.0 • Traditional Score: 1.0 • Verdict: WOKE • Margin: 19.0

Genre: Crime Comedy / Satire | Platform: Theatrical | Director: Boots Riley | Distributor: Neon | Rating: R (pervasive language, drug content, brief sexual content)

Cast: Keke Palmer, Naomi Ackie, Taylour Paige, Poppy Liu, Eiza Gonzalez

Boots Riley made Sorry to Bother You in 2018 -- a Marxist nightmare comedy that earned its politics through sheer formal invention. I Love Boosters is more of the same, following a crew of women who organize a shoplifting ring targeting luxury retail chains. Keke Palmer leads with movie-star charisma as the operation's mastermind, and the heist sequences have real energy. But Riley's ideological project is the entire film: the theft is framed as redistribution, the corporations are cartoonishly evil, and the crew's solidarity is explicitly political. At a traditional score of just 1.0, this is essentially pure ideology delivered through a comedy-crime lens. The craft makes it watchable. It does not make it balanced.

#8: Gail Daughtry and the Celebrity Sex Pass (2026)

Woke Score: 17.6 • Traditional Score: 1.5 • Verdict: WOKE • Margin: 16.1

Cast: Zoey Deutch, Jon Hamm, John Slattery, Sabrina Impacciatore, Ben Wang

A road-trip comedy that runs its horny premise into the ground, David Wain's latest delivers consistent laughs at the cost of any moral coherence whatsoever. Zoey Deutch commits fully as Gail, a Kansas hairdresser whose journey to Los Angeles to sleep with Jon Hamm becomes a vortex of briefcase mix-ups, hairdresser-convention shootouts, and celebrity cameos that range from inspired to puzzling. The film's sexual ethics are cheerfully nihilistic; the only moral position it takes is that traditional sexual morality is a joke. At a traditional score of just 1.5, the near-total absence of countervailing values makes the film's ideological signature clear even though it never lectures. The comedy works. It also works as a delivery system for a worldview.

#9: Scarpetta (2026)

Woke Score: 58.0 • Traditional Score: 42.0 • Verdict: WOKE • Margin: 16.0

Genre: Thriller | Platform: Theatrical

Scarpetta is a pre-release assessment, and the scores reflect our prediction based on available trailers, creative team history, and pre-release information. Patricia Cornwell's forensic pathologist has sold over 120 million copies worldwide -- a quiet titan of American crime fiction beloved by exactly the kind of reader Hollywood usually ignores. The adaptation brings Dr. Kay Scarpetta to the screen with a cast built for prestige, but the early indicators suggest the production has updated the character's politics for the current moment in ways that will shift the ideological balance. At a projected 58 woke to 42 traditional, this is the highest raw woke score on the list, driven by the forensic-procedural framework that inherently raises questions about institutional trust. #11: The Drama (2026)

Woke Score: 22.7 • Traditional Score: 8.4 • Verdict: WOKE • Margin: 14.2

Genre: Dark Comedy / Romance / Drama | Platform: Theatrical | Director: Kristoffer Borgli | Distributor: A24 | Rating: R

Cast: Zendaya, Robert Pattinson, Alana Haim, Mamoudou Athie, Hailey Gates

Kristoffer Borgli, the Norwegian provocateur behind Dream Scenario, has made a film with a single devastating premise: what happens when you discover the person you love once planned to murder children at their school? The answer, as it unfolds through Zendaya and Robert Pattinson's characters, is a dark comedy that interrogates whether we can ever truly know another person -- and whether the attempt is even worth making. Borgli's direction is precise and unsettling. Zendaya gives one of her most controlled performances. But the film's ideological framework is clear: no institution, no relationship, and no moral framework can be trusted to survive scrutiny. The 22.7 woke score reflects a worldview in which every certainty is suspect, a position that aligns neatly with progressive skepticism toward traditional structures.

The Invite is the best-directed film Olivia Wilde has made, a brittle, frequently hilarious dinner-party dramedy that doubles as an autopsy of modern marriage. It is also a film that assumes, from its opening epigraph to its closing moments, that traditional marriage is a prison, monogamy is a slow death, and the only honest response is to blow up the arrangement and see what survives. Seth Rogen brings surprising depth as a husband who thought he was happy. Penelope Cruz and Edward Norton play the couple whose dinner invitation triggers the unraveling. At 17.2 woke to just 3.2 traditional, the margin reflects a film that treats the institution of marriage as its antagonist. The craft is sharp. The comedy lands. Girls Like Girls is exactly what it advertises itself to be, and that is both its most honest quality and its most important characteristic to understand upfront. Hayley Kiyoko built a decade of her career on this story: the 2015 song, the music video, the 2023 novel, and now the feature film. It is a coming-of-age romance about two young women discovering their attraction to each other in a world that would prefer they did not. Maya da Costa and Myra Molloy have genuine chemistry, and Kiyoko's direction is confident in its emotional beats. At 16.8 woke to 4.2 traditional, the margin reflects a film whose entire narrative architecture is built on the premise that queer love is beautiful and the forces opposing it are unjust. Is God Is arrives as one of the most explicitly ideological films of the year. Director Aleshea Harris has been clear about what she is making: a Black feminist revenge myth. A film about women's violent agency against a patriarch who destroyed their family. Twin sisters, scarred by childhood burns, journey across the American South to confront the father who gave them those scars. #18: Wuthering Heights (2026)

Woke Score: 36.0 • Traditional Score: 26.0 • Verdict: WOKE • Margin: 10.0

Genre: Drama | Platform: Theatrical

This adaptation of Emily Bronte's Wuthering Heights sits at a fascinating ideological intersection: a woke score of 36.0 and a traditional score of 26.0. The traditional elements are substantial because Bronte's novel is inherently traditional in its architecture -- all-consuming romantic love as life's defining force, moral consequences that follow moral failure, class distinctions depicted as real and consequential. But the adaptation layers progressive elements on top: female sexuality as liberation, anti-traditional-institution framing, and the kind of provocations that announce a directorial thesis about desire and power. At exactly 10.0 margin, this is the film where the WOKE tier meets the WOKE LEAN tier, and the dual 36/26 scores tell the story of a film pulling in two directions at once.

Cast: Margot Robbie, Jacob Elordi, Hong Chau, Shazad Latif, Alison Oliver

Emerald Fennell's Wuthering Heights is a visually stunning, emotionally aggressive adaptation that adds a BDSM encounter between servants, an extended masturbation sequence on the moors, and an opening public hanging with a visible erection -- none of which appear in Emily Bronte's novel. Margot Robbie is ferociously good as Cathy, finding the character's essential contradiction and playing all three registers at once. Jacob Elordi's Heathcliff is slower to ignite but lands hard. At 35 woke to 26 traditional, the margin of just 9.0 reflects the genuine tug-of-war within the film: Bronte's traditional architecture (all-consuming love, moral consequences, class as structural reality) pushes against Fennell's progressive additions (sexuality as liberation, marriage as cage, transgression as artistic statement). This is the most balanced film in the WOKE LEAN tier, and the 26 traditional score is the highest on this entire list. The question is whether the traditional elements survive Fennell's determination to provoke.

Woke Score: 11.0 • Traditional Score: 3.0 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: 8.0

Season 1 earned enormous trust through grounded storytelling and earned emotional beats. Season 2 leverages that trust to introduce ideological reframing that would not have survived scrutiny if presented upfront. What made the first season compelling -- moral complexity, survival-driven choices, earned relationships -- is gradually replaced by identity-driven narrative restructuring. Pedro Pascal and Bella Ramsey remain exceptional performers, and the production values are HBO at its peak. Director Dee Rees brings formidable craft and genuine humanity to Butterfly Dreams, a coming-of-age drama about a sixteen-year-old trans girl named Maya who leaves her conservative religious hometown in rural Kentucky to live with her estranged grandmother in Louisville and attend an inclusive arts high school. The film centers Maya's self-discovery and the loving relationships that allow her to become herself. The cinematography is warm and intimate. The score is delicate and moving. #25: Forbidden Fruits (2026)

Woke Score: 27.8 • Traditional Score: 21.2 • Verdict: WOKE LEAN • Margin: 6.6

Genre: Comedy Horror | Platform: Theatrical / Shudder

There is a store at the Highland Place mall called Free Eden. It sells cupcake-scented candles, charm bracelets, and the kind of overpriced cotton sundress that costs more than your rent. The employees are gorgeous. They have their own slang. And at some point after closing time, they gather in a candlelit upper room called Paradise and perform rituals in service of what may or may not be actual witchcraft. Forbidden Fruits, the debut feature from writer-director Meredith Alloway, is a comedy horror that satirizes consumer culture, performative feminism, and the commodification of spirituality -- all while delivering genuine genre thrills. At 27.8 woke to 21.2 traditional, the margin of just 6.6 makes this the most balanced entry on the list. The traditional elements are real: genuine friendship, moral consequences for bad behavior, and a climax that takes witchcraft seriously as a threat rather than a lifestyle brand. Forbidden Fruits earns its WOKE LEAN through the strength of its countervailing traditional elements.

Read the full VirtueVigil review of Forbidden Fruits

The Takeaway

Six STRONGLY WOKE films, fourteen WOKE, and five WOKE LEAN -- and the year is only half over. That distribution is not a statistical fluke. It is a structural feature of how the industry operates in 2026. When Steven Spielberg, Boots Riley, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Greta Gerwig, Olivia Wilde, Kristoffer Borgli, and David Lowery all release films on this list within the first six months of the year, the pattern is not about a few activist directors pushing an agenda. The pattern is about the cultural water every filmmaker swims in.

The prestige pipeline deserves particular attention. A24 distributed six of the top 25 entries -- The Moment, The Drama, The Invite, Mother Mary, and more. Neon contributed I Love Boosters and Leviticus. Focus Features released three. This is not fringe filmmaking. This is the center of American independent and prestige cinema, and it is ideologically uniform in its output. Conservative audiences who assume indie cinema offers an alternative to Hollywood's messaging will find no refuge here.

What separates the bottom of this list from the top is not the absence of progressive ideas but the presence of countervailing ones. Wuthering Heights (Emerald Fennell) carries a 26.0 traditional score alongside its 35.0 woke score -- the tug-of-war between Bronte's traditional architecture and Fennell's progressive additions makes it the most ideologically complex entry on the list. Forbidden Fruits earns its 21.2 traditional score through genuine friendship, moral consequences, and a climax that treats witchcraft as a threat. Butterfly Dreams earns its 11.2 traditional score through the grandmother's love and the discipline of artistic community. The films at the top -- The Moment, Disclosure Day, The Bride! -- offer no such counterweight. They are arguments first and entertainment second, however well-made the entertainment is.

The horror genre's presence in the top ten is notable. Leviticus uses the genre to argue religious communities are monstrous. The Bride! reimagines a Universal monster as a feminist romance. Is God Is turns revenge into a Black feminist myth. Horror, which once offered escape from sermonizing, has become one of its primary delivery mechanisms. When horror films carry explicit political agendas, audiences should understand the landscape before they buy a ticket.

The television entries tell their own story. The Pitt: Season 2, Daredevil: Born Again Season 2, The Last of Us Season 2, and Furious: Season 1 all appear on this list -- and all are second seasons. The pattern is consistent across platforms and genres: first seasons build trust with broad audiences, and second seasons spend that trust on ideological commitments. Viewers who enjoyed these shows' first seasons deserve to know what changed.

2026 is on pace to match or exceed 2025's ideological output, but the character of that output has shifted. Last year was defined by animation and genre films that smuggled politics inside popular packaging. This year is defined by prestige auteurs making films whose politics are the marquee. The question for the second half of 2026 is whether audiences continue to show up. The early box office indicators suggest they are increasingly selective. The industry's response to that selectivity will determine whether the back half of this list looks different from the front.
